entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Diaeus of Megalopolis was the final strategos (general) of the Achaian League, a federal state of ancient Greek city-states, whose confrontational policies directly provoked the decisive Roman intervention that led to the League's dissolution and the effective end of Greek independence in 146 BCE. His leadership from 150-149 BCE and again from 148 BCE until his death in 145 BCE marked the ultimate, tragic climax of the struggle between the declining autonomy of Greek poleis and the ascendant power of the Roman Republic. He personified the desperate, yet ultimately futile, resistance against Roman hegemony, culminating in the Achaian War.

Diaeus first rose to prominence following the death of Callicrates in 150 BCE, inheriting a political landscape deeply fractured by pro-Roman and anti-Roman factions. His initial term as strategos from 150 to 149 BCE saw him embroiled in a bitter dispute with Sparta over territorial claims, a conflict he escalated by appealing to Rome, paradoxically accelerating Roman involvement in Greek affairs. After an interval, he was re-elected strategos for 148-146 BCE. It was during this second term that Diaeus, driven by a fervent, if misguided, sense of Greek pride and a desire to consolidate the League's power, adopted increasingly provocative anti-Roman stances. He aggressively pursued the annexation of Sparta and other Peloponnesian cities, defying Roman directives and mistreating Roman envoys, actions that Rome interpreted as direct challenges to its established authority.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Diaeus's leadership as the final strategos of the Achaian League directly provoked the Achaian War, leading to the dissolution of the League and the formal end of Greek independence after centuries of self-rule. His actions ensured Greece's absorption into the Roman Republic as the province of Achaea.
